system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2151-01-11 20:10:00 to 2151-01-12 20:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, chronic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and a history of gastrointestinal bleeding was admitted after his left upper extremity arteriovenous graft failed due to thrombosis. He presented from dialysis with no thrill or bruit but no pain or infection signs. He was hyperkalemic on arrival and received emergent dialysis via a temporary femoral catheter. The next day, he underwent a thrombectomy with mechanical and chemical thrombolysis, which successfully restored graft patency. The procedure was briefly complicated by transient hypoxia and chest pain, attributed to a small pulmonary embolism, which resolved without intervention. He remained alert and stable, with resolution of hyperkalemia and successful dialysis through the restored graft. He was restarted on CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea and discharged to extended care with follow-up appointments in cardiology and sleep medicine. His medications, including insulin, diltiazem, and neuropathy regimen, were continued without major changes.
problems: Other complications due to renal dialysis device, implant, and graft
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Other dependence on machines, supplemental oxygen

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having some pain in your left arm during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started a few weeks ago. My hand gets cold and tingly when I'm on the machine. It goes away once I'm disconnected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like steal syndrome. It happens when too much blood flows through your fistula and not enough stays in your hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it gets worse. The tissue in your hand might not get enough oxygen. That’s why we’re here—to fix it before that happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. So what do we do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to do a procedure tomorrow called fistula banding. We’ll slightly narrow the fistula so more blood stays in your hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under anesthesia, so you won’t feel anything during the surgery. Afterward, you might have some soreness, but we’ll manage that with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I’ve had surgeries before, so I know the drill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll monitor you closely. You’re on dialysis three times a week, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every Monday, Wednesday, Friday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do dialysis tomorrow after your procedure, just to keep your levels stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. My potassium was high last time—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs tonight—your potassium is 6.4, which is high, but you’re not having symptoms like muscle weakness or heart issues, so we’re not alarmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I didn’t feel different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you get a longer dialysis session tomorrow to bring it down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart—should I be concerned with the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have atrial fibrillation and a history of heart issues, so we’ll monitor your rhythm closely. But your heart function is stable, and we’ve cleared you for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had chest pain before with cocaine, but I haven’t used in years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your history. We’re glad you’re clean now. That helps your overall health a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’m trying to stay on track. This dialysis and everything—it keeps me focused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll get you prepped for surgery first thing in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Ready for your procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: As ready as I’ll ever be. Nervous, but I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. The banding was successful. We narrowed the fistula just enough. You’re in recovery now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s awesome. My hand feels normal so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your pulses and sensation—they’re strong and intact. No signs of reduced blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When do I get dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later this morning. We’ll do a longer session to manage your potassium, which was high yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. Everything went smoothly. Your potassium is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel fine. No cramps or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your hand still has good color, warmth, and movement. The banding is working as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call us if you have increasing pain, numbness, coldness, or if your hand changes color. Also, monitor your weight—call if you gain more than three pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds—should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take all your home medications unless we told you otherwise. Especially your blood pressure, diabetes, and heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have insulin and gabapentin for nerve pain—those are fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue both. And use the oxycodone every four hours if you need it for pain—don’t wait until it’s severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see the transplant surgery clinic in a few days. They’ll check your fistula and make sure it’s healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sleep apnea? I forgot my CPAP at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sleep medicine recommends you get re-evaluated. Make sure to follow up with them—good sleep helps your heart and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll ask the facility to help me set that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you to your extended care facility today in stable condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep up the good work with your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m trying. One day at a time.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with left arm pain due to worsening steal syndrome in his left brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula. He underwent elective fistula banding the following day, which was successful in reducing blood flow to alleviate symptoms while preserving access function. He remained asymptomatic postoperatively with no neurovascular deficits. His potassium was elevated at 6.4 on admission but decreased after an extended hemodialysis session. He tolerated a regular diet, maintained baseline functional status, and was discharged in stable condition to an extended care facility. Follow-up was arranged with transplant surgery and sleep medicine. Home medications were resumed, and discharge instructions included monitoring for arm symptoms, weight changes, and dialysis access issues.
